newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU SEALS DEAL ON NORDIC CURBS ON ALCOHOL IMPORTS.
newsitem.headline: EU SEALS DEAL ON NORDIC CURBS ON ALCOHOL IMPORTS.

text.p: EU finance ministers agreed on Monday to let the Nordic member states keep restrictions on the amounts of alcohol and cigarettes travellers may bring home from elsewhere in the bloc until after the turn of the century.
Under the deal reached at a meeting in Brussels, Finland and Denmark will phase out their travel allowance curbs by December 31, 2003.

Sweden -- which refused to agree a final date for ending its restrictions -- will be allowed to keep its present exemption from EU single market rules until June 30, 2000, when it will be reviewed by the EU again.
In effect, Sweden has bought itself extra time as it has not already had to agree a final deadline for lifting the limits, as the European Commission had demanded.
The ministers also agreed on a declaration saying that if Sweden in the end obtained a more favourable final date for its rules, then that date would also be applied to Denmark and Finland.
"So all three countries are very happy with the result," Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink told a press conference.

Stockholm had earlier said it was prepared to go to the European Court of Justice rather than accept a final date for ending travel allowances, saying they are vital for its social and health policies.
But the European Commission says they go against the rules of the single market, in which goods are supposed to flow freely.

So last month it proposed that Denmark, Finland and Sweden phase out their limits on the amount of alcohol and cigarettes that people may bring home by June 30, 2002. In the end, Denmark and Finland won another 18 months grace.
The Commission said the Nordic exemptions to EU rules were due to expire by the end of 1996 unless there was a new agreement.
The question of alcohol quotas is sensitive for the Nordic states which have traditionally applied high taxes to alcohol and tobacco to discourage consumption and raise revenue.
Alcohol and tobacco taxes bring in about $2.7 billion annually in Sweden and $2.17 billion in Finland.
As Nordic excise duties on alcohol are much higher than elsewhere in the EU, some fear individual alcohol imports would jump if the Nordics lost their right to restrict the flow.
A Swede is currently allowed to take home one litre of spirits, five litres of wine and 15 litres of beer compared with 10, 90 and 110 litres respectively for other EU citizens.
